papers.title_in_file: Brain Tumor Diagnosis Using Hybrid Quantum Convolutional Neural Networks (arXiv 2401.15804v3)
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, section III dataset and circuit description, section IV results, discussion and conclusion.
papers.what_it_is: A simulated hybrid quantum-classical convolutional network for three-class brain tumor classification from MRI slices.

assertions.value: The authors report that the HQCNN achieved 99.16% training accuracy and 91.47% validation accuracy on a publicly available brain tumor dataset.
quotes: the HQCNN achieved 99.16% training accuracy and 91.47% validation accuracy
The model achieves a test accuracy of 91.47%
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on one dataset. The abstract calls 91.47% validation accuracy and the conclusion calls it test accuracy.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper uses the label validation in one place and test in another for the same figure.

assertions.value: The authors state that the dataset comprises 3 064 T1-weighted contrast-enhanced images from 233 patients and that the quantum circuit runs on a four-qubit device in PennyLane's default qubit simulator.
assertions.anchor: Sec. III A Dataset and Sec. III C quantum image processing
quotes: comprises 3 064 T1-weighted contrast-enhanced images extracted from 233 patients
a quantum device with four qubits is initialized using PennyLane
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own dataset and simulated four-qubit circuit, Sec. III A and III C.
assertions.reader_inference: The result comes from a classical simulator, not quantum hardware.

assertions.value: The authors state that the primary challenge lay in differentiating meningioma from glioma, and that further improvements are needed to reduce confusion between visually similar tumor types.
assertions.anchor: Sec. IV E Discussion; Sec. V Conclusion
quotes: the primary challenge lay in differentiating meningioma from glioma
further improvements are needed to reduce confusion between visually similar tumor types
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own statement of a limit of their model, Sec. IV E and Sec. V.

assertions.value: The authors state that HQCNNs have the potential to have much lower computational cost than regular CNNs due to the superposition of qubits that create an exponential speedup.
quotes: HQCNNs have the potential to be much lower due to the superposition of qubits that create an exponential speedup.
assertions.certainty_reason: Asserted in the introduction without a computed speedup in the paper. The experiments run on a classical simulator.

papers.title_in_file: Syndrome decoding by quantum approximate optimization (arXiv 2207.05942v2)
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, section V numerical simulation set-up, conclusion.
papers.what_it_is: A simulation study of QAOA used as a syndrome decoder for classical and quantum error-correcting codes.

assertions.value: The authors report simulation results in which the level-4 check-based QAOA decoding of the [7,4,3] Hamming code and the level-4 generator-based QAOA decoding of the [[5,1,3]] quantum code match the maximum likelihood decoding performance.
quotes: We evaluate the level-4 check-based QAOA decoding of the [7,4,3] Hamming code, as well as the level-4 generator-based QAOA decoding of the [[5,1,3]] quantum code.
the simulation results demonstrate that the decoding performances match those of the maximum likelihood decoding
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result for two small codes.

assertions.value: The authors state that they used a classical computer to optimize the parameters and simulate the quantum evaluation, which limits their simulations for large code lengths because the complexity grows exponentially with the number of qubits simulated.
quotes: We used a classical computer to optimize the parameters and simulate the quantum evaluation.
This approach limits our current simulations for large code lengths, as the complexity grows exponentially with the number of qubits simulated.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own statement of the limit of their simulations, Sec. VI.

assertions.value: The authors report that QAOA has the ability to identify degenerate errors of comparable weight, providing multiple potential solutions that match the given syndrome with comparable probabilities, and that QAOA generated a solution distribution in which the probability of each optimal solution was relatively high.
quotes: QAOA has the intriguing ability to identify degenerate errors of comparable weight, providing multiple potential solutions that match the given syndrome with comparable probabilities
QAOA generated a solution distribution in which the probability of each optimal solution was relatively high
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation observation on a few specific error syndromes of the Shor code.

papers.title_in_file: Stochastic noise can be helpful for variational quantum algorithms (arXiv 2210.06723v3)
papers.version_note: File name carries the v1 title (Noise can be helpful for variational quantum algorithms). The text is v3 with the record's title.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, preliminaries, theorem statements, conclusion and outlook, appendix figure captions.
papers.what_it_is: A theory and numerics paper showing that shot noise in gradient estimates can help variational quantum algorithms escape strict saddle points.

assertions.value: The authors state that they prove convergence guarantees and argue that the natural stochasticity of variational algorithms can be beneficial for avoiding strict saddle points.
quotes: We prove convergence guarantees and present practical examples in numerical simulations and on quantum hardware.
We argue that the natural stochasticity of variational algorithms can be beneficial for avoiding strict saddle points
assertions.certainty_reason: The guarantee rests on Theorem 13, which the paper takes from Ref. [24] and adapts with its own Theorem 14. The coordinator may upgrade after checking the proofs.

assertions.value: The authors state that their results focus specifically on shot noise, and that the noise in their theorems is not the generic quantum noise from interaction with the environment, which can be substantially detrimental to the performance of the algorithm.
quotes: It is worth stressing that our results focus specifically on shot noise, which can help in overcoming saddle points.
noise does not mean the generic quantum noise that results from the interaction with the environment
which can be substantially detrimental to the performance of the algorithm
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of the scope of its theorems, Introduction and Conclusion.

assertions.value: The authors report that in a four-qubit simulation with 1000 randomly sampled initial points, gradient descent got trapped by saddle points in 305 cases.
quotes: with four qubits, where 1000 initial points have been sampled randomly.
We have found that in 305 cases (labeled in red), the gradient descent gets trapped by saddle points.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result from one setup.

papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, section 3 NISQ discussion, section 5 challenges, conclusion.
papers.what_it_is: A review of quantum algorithms for supervised learning, written from a classical machine learning perspective.

assertions.value: The author states that the paper aims to provide a classical perspective on current quantum algorithms for supervised learning, and examines the QML literature from a traditional standpoint.
quotes: This paper aims to provide a classical perspective on current quantum algorithms for supervised learning
In this paper, we examine the QML literature from a traditional standpoint
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own aim and scope, Abstract and Sec. 1.
assertions.reader_inference: It is a literature review, not an experiment.

assertions.value: The author states that the current state of research does not definitively favor quantum models over classical ones, and that the true potential of quantum advantage may only be realized with the availability of fault-tolerant quantum computers.
quotes: the current state of research does not definitively favor quantum models over classical ones
The true potential of quantum advantage may only be realized with the availability of fault-tolerant quantum computers.
assertions.certainty_reason: A reviewer's judgment about the state of the literature, not a result in the paper.

assertions.value: The author states that implementing algorithms such as the HHL remains unfeasible given the current state of quantum technology, and that NISQ machines are still not sufficiently powerful to be a credible alternative to classical ones.
quotes: implementing algorithms such as the HHL remains unfeasible given the current state of quantum technology
Such machines, however, are still not sufficiently powerful to be a credible alternative to the classical ones.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's statement about the state of hardware, with no measurement in the paper.

assertions.value: The author states that the standard practice often involves using just a few qubits to demonstrate the viability of a proposed method rather than to showcase any potential advantage.
quotes: the standard practice often involves using just a few qubits to demonstrate the viability of a proposed method rather than to showcase any potential advantage.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's characterization of the literature, not a measured result.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum reinforcement learning in the presence of thermal dissipation (arXiv 2208.06450v2)
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, results discussion of Figs. 2 and 3, conclusions.
papers.what_it_is: An analytical and numerical study of a quantum reinforcement learning protocol for a two-state system under thermal dissipation.

assertions.value: The authors report evidence that dissipation does not significantly degrade the performance of the quantum reinforcement learning protocol for sufficiently low temperatures, being in some cases even beneficial.
quotes: obtaining evidence that dissipation do not significantly degrade the performance of the quantum reinforcement learning protocol for sufficiently low temperatures, being in some cases even beneficial
For sufficiently low temperatures, dissipation does not necessarily have a negative effect on the accuracy of the protocol
assertions.certainty_reason: Result of analytical calculation and numerical simulation for one protocol on a two-state system.

assertions.value: The authors report that in the dissipative case where the protocol fails, the asymptotic mean fidelity is substantially less than without dissipation and the mean exploration parameter does not approach zero, so the protocol does not converge.
assertions.anchor: Sec. III discussion of Fig. 2(b) and (d)
quotes: the asymptotic values of F (k) in the large iteration limit are substantially less than in the absence of dissipation
W (k) does not approach zero as k increases
the protocol does not converge
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical result from one set of simulation parameters. The temperature threshold is in Fig. 3 and is not quoted here.

assertions.value: The authors state that the aim of the work is not to analyze the scalability or speedup of the protocol but the effect of thermal dissipation, and that the environment is modeled by Lindblad dynamics for a two-state system in contact with a thermal bath.
quotes: the aim of this work is not to analyze the scalability or speedup of this type of protocols
we introduced a Lindblad dynamics for the density operator of a two-state system in contact with a thermal bath
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own scope and model, Sec. I and Sec. IV.

papers.title_in_file: Hamiltonian Learning in Quantum Field Theories (arXiv 2401.01308v1)
papers.what_it_is: A protocol, with theory, simulation and experimental data, for learning effective field theory Hamiltonians from measurements on a quantum gas.

assertions.value: The authors state that learning the Hamiltonian for varying spatial measurement resolutions gives access to field theories at different energy scales and allows learning a flow of Hamiltonians reminiscent of the renormalization group.
quotes: Learning the Hamiltonian for varying spatial measurement resolutions gives access to field theories at different energy scales
allows to learn a flow of Hamiltonians reminiscent of the renormalization group
assertions.certainty_reason: Result of theory and numerical studies, with one experimental data set.

assertions.value: The authors report applying the protocol to experimental data of tunnel-coupled superfluids, learning the Hamiltonian of a relativistic classical field theory in thermal equilibrium, with findings consistent with the emergence of a sine-Gordon field theory.
quotes: Our experimental findings are consistent with the emergence of a sine-Gordon field theory.
Hamiltonian of a relativistic classical field theory in thermal equilibrium.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one available experimental data set.

assertions.value: The authors state that the results show the qualitatively expected features, and that they further indicate the experimental challenges with respect to the required system size, measurement resolution and sample size.
quotes: While the results show the qualitatively expected features
they further indicate the experimental challenges with respect to the required system size, measurement resolution and sample size
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own statement of the limits of their experimental demonstration, Sec. VI.

papers.title_in_file: Variational Quantum Algorithms for Differential Equations on a Noisy Quantum Computer (arXiv 2405.02069v2)
papers.version_note: File name carries the v1 title (Quantum Circuit Learning on NISQ Hardware). The text is v2, published in IEEE TQE with the record's title.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, hardware details section, conclusion.
papers.what_it_is: A hardware and simulation study of quantum circuit learning with the parameter shift rule on an IBM quantum computer, applied to function learning and differential equations.

assertions.value: The authors report that they can successfully learn different functions with three-qubit circuits, and that hardware errors accumulate with increasing number of qubits so that only a fraction of the qubits available on current quantum systems can be effectively used.
quotes: we can successfully learn different functions with three-qubit circuits
the hardware errors accumulate with increasing number of qubits and thus only a fraction of the qubits available on the current quantum systems can be effectively used
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from experiments on one IBM device.

assertions.value: The authors report that the parameter shift rule results in higher errors which limits its execution to low-order derivatives, and that a simple differential equation could be solved to a certain extent on ibmq_ehningen.
quotes: The parameter shift rule results in higher errors which limits its execution to low-order derivatives.
a simple differential equation could be solved to a certain extent on ibmq_ehningen
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from experiments on one IBM device.

assertions.value: The authors state that the QCL circuits were executed on the ibmq_ehningen quantum computer, which is a 27-qubit superconducting IBM system.
quotes: The QCL circuits will be executed on the ibmq_ehningen quantum computer.
This system is a 27-qubit superconducting IBM quantum
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental hardware, Sec. III.

assertions.value: The authors state that the solution of a coupled differential equation is demonstrated on a simulator.
quotes: demonstrate the solution of a coupled differential equation on a simulator
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of where this result was obtained, Abstract.
assertions.reader_inference: The coupled-equation result is not a hardware result.

papers.title_in_file: Photonic quantum generative adversarial networks for classical data (arXiv 2405.06023v2)
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, model and simulation sections in part, section III F physical experiment, discussion and future work.
papers.what_it_is: A photonic quantum GAN with a variational linear-optics generator, trained on reduced MNIST in simulation and on Quandela's Ascella processor.

assertions.value: The authors report that the model can learn to generate images, shown by training it end-to-end experimentally on a single-photon quantum processor.
quotes: We demonstrate that the model can learn to generate images by training the model end-to-end experimentally on a single-photon quantum processor.
demonstrating the experimental feasibility of photonic QGANs.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors are from Quandela and run the experiment on Quandela's own processor.

assertions.value: The authors state that, to make the duration of the experiment tractable, they decreased the total number of training iterations to 1000, with 3 SPSA steps for the generator at each iteration, for a total of 3000 SPSA steps.
quotes: In order to make the duration of the experiment tractable, we decrease the total number of training iterations to 1000, with 3 SPSA steps for the generator at each iteration, which results in a total of 3000 SPSA steps.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental set-up, Sec. III F.

assertions.value: The authors state that a point that would require improvements in future experiments is that the generated images do not present a lot of diversity.
quotes: A point that would require improvements in future experiments is that the generated images do not present a lot
which might be improved by adding more encoding phase-shifters into the ansatz.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own statement of a limit of their experimental result, Sec. III F.

assertions.value: The authors state that, to the best of their knowledge, their experiment is the first demonstration of a photonic GAN with a fully quantum generator for classical data.
assertions.anchor: Sec. IV Discussion and future work
quotes: To the best of our knowledge, our experiment is the first demonstration of a photonic GAN with a fully quantum generator for classical data.
assertions.certainty_reason: A priority claim by the authors, who work at the company that built the processor.
